domain.title: Microservices, serverless or a modular monolith?
domain.intro: A recommendation for your team, from Alok Sharan's diagram and the heuristics of the post that goes with it.
domain.author: Alok Sharan
domain.sourceTitle: Microservices VS Serverless VS Modular Monolith
domain.optionsTitle: The three styles, from the diagram

criteria.label: Team size
criteria.definition: The number of developers who build and run the system.

answers.label: Small
answers.definition: 1 to 3 developers.

answers.label: Medium
answers.definition: 4 to 10 developers.

answers.label: Large
answers.definition: More than 10 developers.

criteria.label: Number of teams
criteria.definition: The number of separate teams that work on the system, each with its own backlog.

answers.label: One
answers.definition: A single team works on the whole system.

answers.label: Two or three
answers.definition: Two or three teams share the system.

answers.label: More than three
answers.definition: More than three teams share the system.

criteria.label: Domain separation
criteria.definition: How independent the business areas of the system are from each other.

answers.label: Connected
answers.definition: The business areas share data and change together.

answers.label: Partly separate
answers.definition: Some business areas could stand alone, others share data and change together.

answers.label: Clearly separate
answers.definition: Each business area could be built and released by a different team.

criteria.label: Traffic
criteria.definition: How the load from users changes over time.

answers.label: Steady
answers.definition: The load stays about the same.

answers.label: Spiky, at known times
answers.definition: The load has peaks at times the team knows in advance.

answers.label: Unpredictable
answers.definition: The load has peaks the team cannot foresee.

criteria.label: Background work
criteria.definition: Work the system does that a user request does not trigger.

answers.label: None
answers.definition: All work happens in answer to a user request.

answers.label: Scheduled or event-driven jobs
answers.definition: Jobs that run on a schedule or when an event happens.

answers.label: Heavy, continuous processing
answers.definition: Processing that runs all the time, such as streams or queues with constant load.

criteria.label: Platform
criteria.definition: The cloud or hosting the team already uses.

answers.label: AWS
answers.definition: Amazon Web Services.

answers.label: Azure
answers.definition: Microsoft Azure.

answers.label: Google Cloud
answers.definition: Google Cloud Platform.

answers.label: Cloudflare
answers.definition: Cloudflare's developer platform.

answers.label: On premises
answers.definition: The team's own servers or data centre.

answers.label: Other
answers.definition: Another cloud or hosting provider.

criteria.label: Expected scale
criteria.definition: How much the usage of the system is expected to grow.

answers.label: Low
answers.definition: Usage stays small, for example an internal tool.

answers.label: Medium
answers.definition: Usage grows steadily, within what one deployment can serve.

answers.label: High
answers.definition: Usage is expected to grow a lot, beyond what one deployment can serve.

criteria.label: Operations maturity
criteria.definition: The team's experience running distributed systems in production: monitoring, tracing, on-call, orchestration.

answers.label: Low
answers.definition: Little or no experience running distributed systems.

answers.label: Medium
answers.definition: Some experience, for example with managed cloud services.

answers.label: High
answers.definition: The team already runs and monitors many services or a container orchestrator.

choice.label: Microservices: scale, ownership and domain boundaries justify the operational cost
choice.quote: Move to microservices when scale, ownership, and domain boundaries justify the operational cost.
choice.explanation: Scale: high expected growth or a large team. Ownership: more than one team. Domain boundaries: business areas that could be built and released by different teams. The operational cost is justified only for a team that already runs distributed systems.

choice.label: Modular monolith: start with modular clarity
choice.explanation: For many startups, internal tools, and early-stage products, this is often the smartest starting point.

additions.label: Serverless for scheduled and event-driven jobs
additions.explanation: Serverless works well for automation, background jobs and integrations.

additions.label: Serverless for the parts with unpredictable traffic
additions.quote: It works well for automation, lightweight APIs, background jobs, integrations, and unpredictable traffic patterns.
additions.explanation: Serverless scales automatically and handles traffic spikes; watch provider limits, cold starts and quotas.

cautions.label: Microservices would fit, but not yet
cautions.quote: Move to microservices when scale, ownership, and domain boundaries justify the operational cost.
cautions.explanation: Scale, teams and domains point to microservices, but the team has little experience running distributed systems: service communication, distributed tracing, network failures and security across services. Build that experience first.

cautions.label: Keep continuous processing off serverless
cautions.explanation: Serverless costs per execution: for processing that runs all the time, always-running infrastructure costs less. The post warns of cost surprises if usage grows in the wrong pattern.
